Augment
awg-MENT
v.
From Latin augmentare (to increase), from augere (to increase); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' rebuke of the tribes of Reuben and Gad for provoking the LORD's continued anger.

Biblical Definition

An increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel.

Augment appears once in the Authorized Version, in Moses' sharp rebuke to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, who requested to settle east of the Jordan rather than cross over with the rest of Israel to take the promised inheritance. Moses reads their request against the backdrop of the previous generation's failure at Kadesh-barnea, when the spies' evil report provoked the LORD to swear that generation would die in the wilderness rather than see the land. Now, addressing the sons of that same faithless generation, Moses charges them with rising up in your fathers' stead, an increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel — a warning that a new generation could repeat, and even intensify, the very unfaithfulness that had already cost their fathers forty years. Augment names the specific danger of compounding an existing provocation rather than starting fresh; Moses' fear is not that Reuben and Gad will commit some wholly new sin but that they will add to a wrath already kindled, making a bad situation worse rather than better.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from AUGMENT: to increase; to make larger or greater; here of provoking the LORD's already-kindled anger to increase further.

expand to see more

AUGMENT, v.t. To increase; to enlarge in size, extent, or quantity.

AUGMENT, v.i. To grow larger; to increase.

In Numbers 32:14 the word names the danger of adding to an already-provoked divine anger.

Moses charges Reuben and Gad with rising up as 'an increase of sinful men' after their fathers.

The rebuke is answered by the tribes' immediate pledge to fight alongside their brethren for the conquest.

Key Scripture

Num 32:14 — "And, behold, ye are risen up in your fathers' stead, an increase of sinful men, to augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD toward Israel."

Modern Corruption

There is no live postmodern redefinition of this ordinary word; the entry exists because Moses' charge names a specific, recognizable danger — a new generation compounding rather than correcting an inherited pattern of unfaithfulness — that remains a live warning wherever old provocations are not repented of but repeated.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Augment retains its plain sense of increase; no rival ideology has captured the word.

The principle to recover is Moses' own diagnosis: the danger named is not merely repeating a fathers' sin but augmenting it, adding a fresh generation's provocation onto an anger already kindled by the previous one. Reuben and Gad's swift response — a binding pledge to cross over armed and fight until the conquest is complete — shows the rebuke rightly heard turns a request that could have augmented judgment into renewed covenant faithfulness instead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Augment occurs once, in Moses' rebuke of Reuben and Gad, warning that their request could compound rather than correct the unfaithfulness of the previous wilderness generation.

expand to see more

Augment in Numbers 32:14 names the danger of adding to an already-kindled divine anger.

Moses ties the tribes' request directly to the failure of the spies at Kadesh-barnea.

The charge 'an increase of sinful men' accuses a new generation of repeating a fathers' pattern.

Reuben and Gad respond with a binding pledge to cross armed and fight for the whole conquest.

Moses accepts the pledge, and the two tribes settle east of Jordan only after Canaan is subdued.

Usage

"To augment yet the fierce anger of the LORD — compounding, not merely repeating, a fathers' provocation."

"An increase of sinful men — a new generation charged with intensifying an old unfaithfulness."

"The rebuke rightly heard turns a request that could have provoked further wrath into renewed obedience."
